deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page records a damping experiment with a magnetometer (bundle 'PH.Induktion'; Gauss–Weber induction work of the 1830s). The needle swings inside a multiplier coil. When the coil circuit is closed, the induced currents damp the swing strongly. When it is open, only air and other residual damping remain. The previous page holds raw turning-point readings and their sums. This page reduces them.

COLUMNS. Each row has four entries:
- n: the oscillation number, in groups 0-2, 10-12, 14-16, 24-26, 28-30, 38-40, 42-44, 52-54, 56-58, 66-68.
- R_n: a scale reading near 1000-1013 that drifts slowly. This is most plausibly the rest position (mean of consecutive turning points).
- A_n: the arc of oscillation in scale divisions, falling from 1389.4 to 274.65.
- L_n = log10(A_n). Example: log10(1389.4) = 3.14282 and log10(1385.95) = 3.14176. All entries I checked are correct to about 1 unit in the 5th decimal.

REDUCTION OF ARCS (right-hand block). For the large arcs Gauss computes a correction c_n and the corrected log L'_n = log10(A_n - c_n). Example: 1389.4 - 10.107 = 1379.293, and log10 of that is 3.13965.

The corrections follow a cubic law, c_n = k*A_n^3 with k ≈ 3.768e-9 (my inference):
- 10.107/1389.4^3 = 3.768e-9
- 9.421/1357.3^3 = 3.768e-9
- 5.693/1147.45^3 = 3.768e-9
- 1.131/669.55^3 = 3.768e-9

This is the standard reduction of mirror-and-scale readings to arcs proportional to angle. A scale reading x = D·tan(ψ) gives the angle as D·arctan(x/D) ≈ x - x^3/(3D^2). If A is the full arc (A = 2x), this becomes A - A^3/(12 D^2). Then k = 1/(12 D^2) gives D ≈ 4700 scale divisions. That interpretation is mine. The point is that only the cubic term is kept, so log decrements are computed for angles, not tangents.

LOGARITHMIC DECREMENTS. All decrements are scaled by 10^5. For two groups of three, ten oscillations apart, Gauss takes (sum of the three logs − sum of the three later logs)/30:
- Open, 0-2 vs 10-12: (9.42529 - 9.39501)/30 = 0.0010093 → 100.93. Corrected logs: (9.41581 - 9.38596)/30 → 99.50.
- Closed, 14-16 vs 24-26: (9.24981 - 8.54812)/30 = 0.023390 → 2338.97. Corrected: (9.24259 - 8.54565)/30 → 2323.13.
- Open, 28-30 vs 38-40: (8.40077 - 8.37779)/30 → 76.60. Gauss gives 76.3 when reduced; this is consistent with the small cubic correction at A ≈ 630, which I estimate at about -0.2.
- Closed, 42-44 vs 52-54: (8.23277 - 7.51804)/30 → 2382.43.
- Open, 56-58 vs 66-68: (7.36452 - 7.32076)/30 → 145.87.

SEPARATING THE INDUCTION DAMPING. From each closed-circuit decrement Gauss subtracts the mean of the open-circuit decrements on either side of it:
- 2338.97 - (100.93 + 76.60)/2 = 2250.205 → 2250.21
- 2382.43 - (76.60 + 145.87)/2 = 2271.195 → 2271.20
- For the reduced values: 2323.13 - (99.50 + 76.3)/2 = 2235.23. Gauss writes 2233.2 (see errors).

2284.14, written beside 76.60, is probably a combined damping value. My best guess, not certain: (2338.97 + 2382.43)/2 - 76.60 = 2284.10.

'Th. 12°3' is the thermometer reading, 12.3°.

The purpose is to isolate the logarithmic decrement caused purely by induced currents, the 'induction damping'. It is the quantity later used by Weber to relate damping to circuit resistance.
errors: The reduced closed-minus-open value is written 2233.2. The consistent value is 2323.13 - (99.50+76.3)/2 = 2235.2, so either Gauss slipped by 2 units or the digit is misread.
2284.14 cannot be reproduced exactly. The nearest natural reconstruction, mean(2338.97, 2382.43) - 76.60, gives 2284.10. Either a different combination was used or there is a small slip.

The open-circuit decrement is not constant (100.93, 76.60, 145.87). Subtracting the mean of the bracketing open values is a reasonable interpolation, not a rigorous correction. The variation may reflect drift of the rest position (1013 → 1000) or amplitude-dependent air damping.
No arithmetic errors were found in the logarithms or in the cubic corrections; all spot checks agree to about 1e-5.

results.what: Logarithmic decrement from groups of three amplitudes ten swings apart: (ΣlogA_early − ΣlogA_late)/30
results.modern_name: logarithmic decrement of a damped oscillator (averaged estimator)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss and Weber, Göttingen magnetic work, 1830s (Gauss, Intensitas 1832; Weber's damping papers)

results.what: Reduction of scale-read arcs by a cubic correction A − kA^3 (arctan reduction for mirror-scale readings)
results.modern_name: reduction of mirror-scale (Poggendorff–Gauss) readings to angle, small-angle arctan correction

results.what: Separating induction damping as closed-circuit decrement minus interpolated open-circuit (air) decrement
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss and Weber, Resultate aus den Beobachtungen des magnetischen Vereins, ca. 1837-1841; Weber later for resistance measurement

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine experimental reduction in the style of the published Gauss–Weber magnetic work: log decrements, arctan correction of mirror readings, and subtraction of air damping. It is a nice unpublished data sheet but contains no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: third column is log10 of the arc
correction c is proportional to A^3 with constant ≈ 3.768e-9
implied scale distance ≈ 4700 divisions if A is the full arc

transcription_corrections: The corrected-log block holds the values c = kA^3 (10.107 …) and log10(A−c). It is a reduction of arcs, not independent data.
Row 28 rest position is 1011.250 (blotted digit); row 14 arc 1279.05 is confirmed by its logarithm.
The top-right '50h/7' is crossed out; the folio number is (7).
'2233.2' may be '2235.2' by the consistent arithmetic; check the image.
The '76.60' struck out near row 26 is a misplaced first entry, rewritten at row 30.
